lines.raw: Brand and generic.
lines.say: Brand and generic.

lines.raw: Lesson 4 showed that every drug has a **generic name** (the active ingredient) and may have a **brand name**.
lines.say: Lesson 4 showed that every drug has a generic name (the active ingredient) and may have a brand name.

lines.raw: This lesson is about the choice between them, and the plan's rules about which drugs it pays for.
lines.say: This lesson is about the choice between them, and the plan's rules about which drugs it pays for.

lines.raw: When a company invents a new drug, it gets a **patent** and is the only one allowed to sell it for some years.
lines.say: When a company invents a new drug, it gets a patent and is the only one allowed to sell it for some years.

lines.raw: That first version is the **brand** drug.
lines.say: That first version is the brand drug.

lines.raw: After the patent ends, other companies can make copies called **generics**, which are usually **much cheaper**.
lines.say: After the patent ends, other companies can make copies called generics, which are usually much cheaper.

lines.raw: Here is a quick table.
lines.say: Here is a quick table.

lines.raw: Example. Brand: **Lipitor**. Generic: **atorvastatin**.
lines.say: Example. Brand: Lipitor. Generic: atorvastatin.

lines.raw: Active ingredient. Brand: Atorvastatin. Generic: Atorvastatin (the same).
lines.say: Active ingredient. Brand: Atorvastatin. Generic: Atorvastatin (the same).

lines.raw: Strength and form. Brand: 20 mg tablet. Generic: 20 mg tablet (the same).
lines.say: Strength and form. Brand: 20 mg tablet. Generic: 20 mg tablet (the same).

lines.raw: Approved by. Brand: FDA. Generic: FDA, which checks it works the same way in the body.
lines.say: Approved by. Brand: F D A. Generic: F D A, which checks it works the same way in the body.

lines.raw: Looks the same? Brand: Its own colour and shape. Generic: May look different (colour, shape, company name).
lines.say: Looks the same? Brand: Its own colour and shape. Generic: May look different (colour, shape, company name).

lines.raw: Price. Brand: Higher. Generic: Usually much lower.
lines.say: Price. Brand: Higher. Generic: Usually much lower.

lines.raw: Most US prescriptions are generics.
lines.say: Most U S prescriptions are generics.

lines.raw: About **9 out of 10** prescriptions filled in the US are for generic drugs.
lines.say: About 9 out of 10 prescriptions filled in the U S are for generic drugs.

lines.raw: Generics make up a much smaller share of the **money**, because brand drugs cost so much more.
lines.say: Generics make up a much smaller share of the money, because brand drugs cost so much more.

lines.raw: In Nepal: The cheaper company's version.
lines.say: In Nepal: The cheaper company's version.

lines.say: With private insurance:

lines.raw: Ram's prescription says a well-known brand of paracetamol.
lines.say: Ram's prescription says a well-known brand of paracetamol.

lines.raw: The medical shop dai says: "Same **salt**, other company, half the price.
lines.say: The medical shop dai says: "Same salt, other company, half the price.

lines.raw: Want this one?".
lines.say: Want this one?".

lines.raw: Ram agrees.
lines.say: Ram agrees.

lines.raw: That is **generic substitution**: same active ingredient and strength, different company, lower price.
lines.say: That is generic substitution: same active ingredient and strength, different company, lower price.

lines.raw: If Ram insists on the exact brand written by the doctor, he pays more.
lines.say: If Ram insists on the exact brand written by the doctor, he pays more.

lines.raw: His insurer may only reimburse up to a reasonable price.
lines.say: His insurer may only reimburse up to a reasonable price.

lines.say: With the Social Security Fund:

lines.raw: Sita's SSF-listed hospital pharmacy usually gives whichever company's version it stocks.
lines.say: Sita's S S F listed hospital pharmacy usually gives whichever company's version it stocks.

lines.raw: Sita rarely gets to choose.
lines.say: Sita rarely gets to choose.

lines.raw: SSF pays according to its approved rates, so cheaper equivalent medicines help both SSF and Sita, who pays 20% of the cost.
lines.say: S S F pays according to its approved rates, so cheaper equivalent medicines help both S S F and Sita, who pays 20 percent of the cost.

lines.raw: In the US, most states allow (and some require) the pharmacist to **swap a brand for an approved generic** unless the doctor or patient says otherwise.
lines.say: In the U S, most states allow (and some require) the pharmacist to swap a brand for an approved generic unless the doctor or patient says otherwise.

lines.raw: The claim records what happened in the **DAW code**.
lines.say: The claim records what happened in the D A W code.

lines.raw: DAW: Dispense As Written.
lines.say: D A W: Dispense As Written.

lines.raw: The most common DAW codes (also called the product selection code).
lines.say: The most common D A W codes (also called the product selection code).

lines.raw: `0`. Meaning: No product selection indicated. Simple example: Normal case: generic dispensed, or a brand that has no generic yet.
lines.say: 0. Meaning: No product selection indicated. Simple example: Normal case: generic dispensed, or a brand that has no generic yet.

lines.raw: `1`. Meaning: Substitution **not allowed by prescriber**. Simple example: Doctor writes "brand medically necessary": must give Lipitor.
lines.say: 1. Meaning: Substitution not allowed by prescriber. Simple example: Doctor writes "brand medically necessary": must give Lipitor.

lines.raw: `2`. Meaning: Substitution allowed, **patient requested** the brand. Simple example: Doctor is fine with generic, but Emily asks for Lipitor.
lines.say: 2. Meaning: Substitution allowed, patient requested the brand. Simple example: Doctor is fine with generic, but Emily asks for Lipitor.

lines.raw: Why DAW 2 costs the patient more.
lines.say: Why D A W 2 costs the patient more.

lines.raw: With **DAW 2**, the patient chose the expensive brand when a cheaper generic was fine.
lines.say: With D A W 2, the patient chose the expensive brand when a cheaper generic was fine.

lines.raw: Many plans then make the patient pay their copay **plus the price difference** between the brand and the generic.
lines.say: Many plans then make the patient pay their copay plus the price difference between the brand and the generic.

lines.raw: With **DAW 1**, the doctor decided, so plans usually do not charge that difference (though some ask for prior authorization).
lines.say: With D A W 1, the doctor decided, so plans usually do not charge that difference (though some ask for prior authorization).

lines.raw: Codes **3 to 9** also exist, for cases such as the generic being out of stock or not available in the market.
lines.say: Codes 3 to 9 also exist, for cases such as the generic being out of stock or not available in the market.

lines.raw: The formulary: the plan's drug list.
lines.say: The formulary: the plan's drug list.

scenes.section: The formulary: the plan's drug list

lines.raw: A **formulary** is the list of drugs a plan covers.
lines.say: A formulary is the list of drugs a plan covers.

lines.raw: The PBM builds it, deciding which drugs are covered and how much the patient pays.
lines.say: The P B M builds it, deciding which drugs are covered and how much the patient pays.

lines.raw: Drugs on the list are placed in **tiers**: the lower the tier, the less the patient pays.
lines.say: Drugs on the list are placed in tiers: the lower the tier, the less the patient pays.

scenes.section: The formulary: the plan's drug list

lines.raw: Emily's plan (a typical example; every plan is different).
lines.say: Emily's plan (a typical example; every plan is different).

lines.raw: **Tier 1**. What goes here: Preferred generics. Emily pays (30-day retail fill): **$5** copay. Example: Amoxicillin, ibuprofen 800 mg, atorvastatin.
lines.say: Tier 1. What goes here: Preferred generics. Emily pays (30-day retail fill): 5 dollars copay. Example: Amoxicillin, ibuprofen 800 mg, atorvastatin.

lines.raw: **Tier 2**. What goes here: Preferred brands. Emily pays (30-day retail fill): **$40** copay. Example: A brand drug with no generic, chosen by the PBM.
lines.say: Tier 2. What goes here: Preferred brands. Emily pays (30-day retail fill): 40 dollars copay. Example: A brand drug with no generic, chosen by the P B M.

lines.raw: **Tier 3**. What goes here: Non-preferred drugs. Emily pays (30-day retail fill): **$75** copay. Example: A brand with a cheaper alternative on tier 1 or 2.
lines.say: Tier 3. What goes here: Non-preferred drugs. Emily pays (30-day retail fill): 75 dollars copay. Example: A brand with a cheaper alternative on tier 1 or 2.

lines.raw: **Tier 4**. What goes here: Specialty drugs. Emily pays (30-day retail fill): **25%** coinsurance, max $250 per fill. Example: Expensive drugs for cancer, multiple sclerosis or rheumatoid arthritis.
lines.say: Tier 4. What goes here: Specialty drugs. Emily pays (30-day retail fill): 25 percent coinsurance, max 250 dollars per fill. Example: Expensive drugs for cancer, multiple sclerosis or rheumatoid arthritis.

lines.raw: Not covered. What goes here: Non-formulary or excluded. Emily pays (30-day retail fill): Full price, unless an exception is approved. Example: Drugs the plan chose not to cover.
lines.say: Not covered. What goes here: Non-formulary or excluded. Emily pays (30-day retail fill): Full price, unless an exception is approved. Example: Drugs the plan chose not to cover.

lines.say: 90-day fills by mail.

lines.say: For medicines taken every day, like atorvastatin, many plans offer a 90-day supply from a mail-order pharmacy for less than three times the 30-day copay.

lines.say: Think of a canteen menu with prices.

lines.raw: Back to the office canteen.
lines.say: Back to the office canteen.

lines.raw: **Dal bhat** is subsidised and cheap (tier 1).
lines.say: Dal bhat is subsidised and cheap (tier 1).

lines.raw: **Momo** costs a bit more (tier 2).
lines.say: Momo costs a bit more (tier 2).

lines.raw: A **pizza** brought in from outside costs a lot (tier 3).
lines.say: A pizza brought in from outside costs a lot (tier 3).

lines.raw: And some items are **not on the menu** at all.
lines.say: And some items are not on the menu at all.

lines.raw: The canteen manager (PBM) decides the menu to keep the office's (plan's) costs down.
lines.say: The canteen manager (P B M) decides the menu to keep the office's (plan's) costs down.

lines.raw: Utilisation management: rules before paying.
lines.say: Utilisation management: rules before paying.

lines.raw: Even if a drug is on the formulary, the plan can add rules.
lines.say: Even if a drug is on the formulary, the plan can add rules.

lines.raw: These are called **utilisation management (UM)**.
lines.say: These are called utilisation management (U M).

lines.raw: If a rule is not met, the claim is **rejected at the counter** (lesson 9).
lines.say: If a rule is not met, the claim is rejected at the counter (lesson 9).

lines.raw: Prior authorization (PA).
lines.say: Prior authorization (P A).

lines.raw: The doctor must get the plan's **approval before** the drug is covered, usually by explaining why the patient needs it.
lines.say: The doctor must get the plan's approval before the drug is covered, usually by explaining why the patient needs it.

lines.raw: Common for expensive or specialty drugs.
lines.say: Common for expensive or specialty drugs.

lines.raw: Step therapy.
lines.say: Step therapy.

lines.raw: The patient must **try a cheaper drug first** (step 1).
lines.say: The patient must try a cheaper drug first (step 1).

lines.raw: Only if it does not work does the plan cover the more expensive drug (step 2).
lines.say: Only if it does not work does the plan cover the more expensive drug (step 2).

lines.raw: Quantity limit.
lines.say: Quantity limit.

lines.raw: A **maximum amount** per fill or per period.
lines.say: A maximum amount per fill or per period.

lines.raw: For example, no more than 30 tablets per 30 days.
lines.say: For example, no more than 30 tablets per 30 days.

lines.raw: In the US: Emily and the formulary.
lines.say: In the U S: Emily and the formulary.

lines.raw: Emily's amoxicillin, ibuprofen and atorvastatin are all **tier 1 generics** with no special rules, so each claim pays straight away.
lines.say: Emily's amoxicillin, ibuprofen and atorvastatin are all tier 1 generics with no special rules, so each claim pays straight away.

lines.raw: If Dr. Patel had prescribed brand **Lipitor** with **DAW 1**, the claim might be rejected for **prior authorization**: the plan wants to know why the generic will not do.
lines.say: If Doctor Patel had prescribed brand Lipitor with D A W 1, the claim might be rejected for prior authorization: the plan wants to know why the generic will not do.

lines.raw: If Emily herself asked for Lipitor (**DAW 2**), the plan would pay, but she would pay more.
lines.say: If Emily herself asked for Lipitor (D A W 2), the plan would pay, but she would pay more.

lines.raw: Key takeaways.
lines.say: Key takeaways.

lines.raw: **Generic** = same active ingredient, strength and form as the brand, FDA-approved, usually much cheaper.
lines.say: Generic = same active ingredient, strength and form as the brand, F D A approved, usually much cheaper.

lines.raw: **DAW 0** = normal, **DAW 1** = doctor says brand only, **DAW 2** = patient chose the brand.
lines.say: D A W 0 = normal, D A W 1 = doctor says brand only, D A W 2 = patient chose the brand.

lines.raw: The **formulary** is the plan's list of covered drugs, sorted into **tiers** with different copays.
lines.say: The formulary is the plan's list of covered drugs, sorted into tiers with different copays.

lines.raw: UM rules (**prior authorization**, **step therapy**, **quantity limits**) can stop a claim at the counter.
lines.say: U M rules (prior authorization, step therapy, quantity limits) can stop a claim at the counter.
